========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, absolutely. Restless doesn't even begin to cover it. If I'm forced to just sit there and not actively work on something, it's almost like physical torture. 

Take IEP meetings, for example. As a special ed teacher, I'm in those all the time. You've got the parents, the school psychologist, maybe the principal or a district rep, everyone sitting around this big conference table for an hour or more, and it's supposed to be this very serious, focused environment. But I just... I can't just sit there. Underneath the table, my leg is going a mile a minute, just bouncing, bouncing, bouncing. And if it's not my leg, I've got a pen in my hand and I'm clicking it, or I'm shifting my weight from one side of the chair to the other, crossing and uncrossing my arms. 

I'm taking some administration classes right now, too, trying to keep my credentials up to date, and it's the exact same thing there. I'll be sitting in the lecture, trying to listen to whatever policy they're talking about, and I'm just squirming in my seat. The worst part is, I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time. It's completely unconscious until I notice the person next to me giving me this look, you know? They glance over at me, or they stare at my hand, and suddenly I realize I've been clicking my pen like a madman or shaking the whole table with my knee for the last ten minutes.

Well, no, not really. I mean, I hear what people are saying just fine. When I'm in those IEP meetings, even if my leg is bouncing or I'm shifting around, I'm still tracking the conversation. I wasn't distracted from what she was saying, I was just... impatient to be doing it. So, no, I wouldn't say I have a hard time focusing on people or following through. It's just the sitting still part that gets me.

I just bounce from one task to the next, at work and at home, and I can never seem to just... shut myself off, you know? It’s honestly exhausting, never being able to power down, but I just can't stop.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel restless when you're not actively doing something?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. But I just... I can't just sit there. Underneath the table, my leg is going a mile a minute, just bouncing, bouncing, bouncing. And if it's not my leg, I've got a pen in my hand and I'm clicking it, or I'm shifting my weight from one side of the chair to the other, crossing and uncrossing my arms. \n\nI'm taking some administration classes right now, too, trying to keep my credentials up to date, and it's the exact same thing there. Well, yes. Yes, it has, and it's... it's actually become quite a serious issue lately, which is hard for me to admit because I've always prided myself on being a very capable, hands-on kind of guy. But the complaints got serious enough that administration actually put me on a corrective action plan. A corrective plan, at 58 years old! I have to have these weekly check-ins now about my "professional presence" and "classroom demeanor," and it's just humiliating. I feel like I'm damaging the trust I've built with my colleagues over the years, and they're looking at me like I'm a liability rather than a partner.

And it's not just at school, either. It's spilling over into my home life, which is... well, it's really stressing my marriage. My wife and I, we help take care of her elderly mother who lives with us. It's a lot of work, a lot of routine—medications, meals, getting her to appointments. I'll start making lunch, but then I'll see the mail needs sorting, so I start doing that, and then I'll notice a loose hinge on the cabinet and go get my tools, and meanwhile, her mother is just sitting there waiting for her soup. My wife told me she feels like she has to manage my energy on top of managing her mother's care, and that's just... it's an awful thing to hear from your spouse. 

I'm trying to help. I really am. In my head, I'm tackling all these tasks that need to be done, I'm being productive, I'm keeping the household running. But the reality is, I'm exhausting the people around me. My wife is frustrated, my colleagues are annoyed, and I just feel this terrible guilt because I can't seem to just dial it back. I want to be a supportive husband and a reliable teacher, but this... this engine inside me just won't shut off, and it's really starting to fray my relationships.

Oh, absolutely. Yes. Without a doubt. I mean, it's really important to me that you understand this isn't just... it's not just some reaction to recent stress, you know? I remember even into middle school and high school, it was the exact same thing. Always the kid who couldn't just sit quietly and listen. It’s just... it’s always been this way. I’ve always had this motor running, always had to be in the mix. So, no, it's definitely not a new development or some mid-life crisis thing. It's just how I've been wired my entire life.

Well, yeah, I mean... like I was just pouring my heart out about a minute ago, it really, really has. I mean, "significantly" is probably the exact right word for it, unfortunately.

Distress? Oh, God, yes. I mean, distress is almost putting it mildly at this point. It's... it's a heavy, heavy weight that I feel like I'm carrying around from the minute I wake up to the minute I finally manage to fall asleep. 

You know, I wake up every morning, and I have these really great intentions. I sit on the edge of the bed and I tell myself, "Okay, today, I'm going to be calm. Today, I'm just going to listen to my co-teachers, I'm going to let my wife handle her mother's breakfast without jumping in and making a mess of the routine." But then the day actually starts, and it's like this switch flips inside my chest, and I'm just going and going and going. I can't stop it. 

And then, at the end of the day, when the house finally quiets down... that's when the distress really hits me the hardest. I'll sit there in my favorite chair in the living room, usually after my wife has already gone to bed because she's just so totally exhausted from dealing with her mom and, frankly, dealing with me. And I just sit there in the quiet and replay the whole day in my head. I think about the looks on the other teachers' faces—you know, that tight-lipped, forced smile they give me when I've interrupted them for the fourth time in a single hour. Or I think about the heavy sigh my wife lets out when she walks into the kitchen and sees I've left a trail of half-finished chores everywhere because I got distracted trying to fix a squeaky floorboard. 

It brings on this profound sense of... of failure, really. Because I'm 58 years old! I should have all of this figured out by now, shouldn't I? I should be the wise, steady senior teacher at school. I should be the rock-solid, dependable husband at home. But instead, I feel like I'm this chaotic force of nature that everyone just has to brace themselves against. It makes me feel incredibly guilty. And honestly, sometimes it makes me feel really, really lonely, even when I'm surrounded by people all day long, because I can literally see them pulling away from me, bracing themselves when I walk into a room. 

So, yes, the distress is... it's very real. It's with me all the time lately. It just completely wears you down, feeling like your very nature, the core of who you are and how you operate, is a burden to the people you care about most in this world.

Just go, go, go. \n\nAnd then I get home, and you’d think I’d sit down in my recliner and watch the news, but no, I walk through the front door and immediately start cleaning the gutters, or I'm pulling everything out of the garage to reorganize the tool bench for the third time this month. I just bounce from one task to the next, at work and at home, and I can never seem to just... shut myself off, you know? It’s honestly exhausting, never being able to power down, but I just can't stop.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel restless when you're not actively doing something?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Restless doesn't even begin to cover it. If I'm forced to just sit there and not actively work on something, it's almost like physical torture. \n\nTake IEP meetings, for example. As a special ed teacher, I'm in those all the time. You've got the parents, the school psychologist, maybe the principal or a district rep, everyone sitting around this big conference table for an hour or more, and it's supposed to be this very serious, focused environment. But I just... I can't just sit there. Underneath the table, my leg is going a mile a minute, just bouncing, bouncing, bouncing. And if it's not my leg, I've got a pen in my hand and I'm clicking it, or I'm shifting my weight from one side of the chair to the other, crossing and uncrossing my arms. \n\nI'm taking some administration classes right now, too, trying to keep my credentials up to date, and it's the exact same thing there. I'll be sitting in the lecture, trying to listen to whatever policy they're talking about, and I'm just squirming in my seat. The worst part is, I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time. It's completely unconscious until I notice the person next to me giving me this look, you know? They glance over at me, or they stare at my hand, and suddenly I realize I've been clicking my pen like a madman or shaking the whole table with my knee for the last ten minutes. \n\nIt's embarrassing, frankly. I'm a 58-year-old professional, I should be able to sit through a standard meeting without fidgeting like one of my middle schoolers, but I just have this pent-up energy that absolutely has to leak out somehow if I'm not up on my feet moving around. I try to stop, I really do, I'll put my hands flat on the table, but two minutes later, I'm tapping my fingers or shifting around all over again.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find it difficult to focus on what's being said or to follow through on instructions?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, I hear what people are saying just fine. When I'm in those IEP meetings, even if my leg is bouncing or I'm shifting around, I'm still tracking the conversation. I'm listening to the parents, I'm taking in what the school psychologist is suggesting about accommodations. I don't really lose the thread of the conversation, you know? \n\nAnd as far as instructions go... well, in my job, I'm usually the one giving them, but even when I'm taking those administration classes I mentioned, I don't have trouble understanding what the professor wants us to do for an assignment. If they say we need to write a ten-page paper on district policy changes, I hear it, I know what I need to do, and I get it done. The problem isn't that I can't focus on what's being asked of me, or that I get confused and forget the steps. It's more just... the physical act of sitting there while the instructions are being given. \n\nLike, last week, my wife asked me to help her put together this new shelving unit for the garage. She was reading the manual, telling me which brackets go where, and I understood her perfectly. I didn't miss a word. But while she was reading, I was already grabbing the drill, pacing around the boxes, sorting the screws, just itching to get my hands on it and start building. I wasn't distracted from what she was saying, I was just... impatient to be doing it. So, no, I wouldn't say I have a hard time focusing on people or following through. It's just the sitting still part that gets me.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking through the consequences?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive in a dangerous or reckless way, like, you know, gambling away the mortgage or buying a sports car on a whim. I'm a planner by nature, especially with my job. You have to be. You can't just wing an IEP for a student with severe behavioral needs, you know? You have to think through every possible scenario, every trigger, every accommodation. And I do that. I'm very thorough. \n\nSo, I don't just act without thinking about the big things. Like with those administration classes I'm taking. I didn't just wake up one morning and decide to enroll. I looked at the district requirements, I talked to my principal about potential career paths, I figured out the tuition costs and how it would fit into my schedule. I mapped the whole thing out. \n\nI guess... maybe I can be a little quick to jump into action, like I was saying about the garage shelves with my wife. I just want to get things moving. If there's a problem, I want to fix it right that second. If one of my students is having a meltdown, I'm right in there, intervening, trying to de-escalate before anyone else even realizes what's happening. But I wouldn't call that acting without thinking of the consequences. I'm thinking of the consequences, I'm just trying to prevent them from getting worse by acting fast. I'm just... I'm a doer. I don't sit back and wait for things to happen, but I'm not reckless about it. I've been doing this a long time, 58 years, and I've always been this way. I just like to keep things moving forward. So, no, I wouldn't say I have a problem with impulse control or ignoring consequences.\n\nDoctor: Has your constant need to be active and moving ever caused problems at work or in your relationships with others?\n\nPatient: Well, yes. Yes, it has, and it's... it's actually become quite a serious issue lately, which is hard for me to admit because I've always prided myself on being a very capable, hands-on kind of guy. But this constant need to be doing something, to be in motion, it's really starting to catch up with me in ways I never anticipated. \n\nAt work, for instance. I mentioned I'm a special ed teacher, and a lot of what I do involves co-teaching or collaborating with other staff members. And apparently, my... my energy, I guess you could call it, has become a real problem. I've had colleagues complain that I'm overwhelming in the classroom. They say I'm always pacing, always jumping in before they finish a sentence, always rearranging things or hovering when they're trying to work one-on-one with a student. It got to the point where a couple of the general ed teachers went to the principal about it. They said I was creating a chaotic environment, which broke my heart because I'm just trying to be involved and helpful. But the complaints got serious enough that administration actually put me on a corrective action plan. A corrective plan, at 58 years old! I have to have these weekly check-ins now about my \"professional presence\" and \"classroom demeanor,\" and it's just humiliating. I feel like I'm damaging the trust I've built with my colleagues over the years, and they're looking at me like I'm a liability rather than a partner.\n\nAnd it's not just at school, either. It's spilling over into my home life, which is... well, it's really stressing my marriage. My wife and I, we help take care of her elderly mother who lives with us. It's a lot of work, a lot of routine—medications, meals, getting her to appointments. And my wife recently sat me down and told me that I'm making it harder for everyone. She said that when I'm supposed to be helping, I'm just a whirlwind. I'll start making lunch, but then I'll see the mail needs sorting, so I start doing that, and then I'll notice a loose hinge on the cabinet and go get my tools, and meanwhile, her mother is just sitting there waiting for her soup. My wife told me she feels like she has to manage my energy on top of managing her mother's care, and that's just... it's an awful thing to hear from your spouse. \n\nI'm trying to help. I really am. In my head, I'm tackling all these tasks that need to be done, I'm being productive, I'm keeping the household running. But the reality is, I'm exhausting the people around me. My wife is frustrated, my colleagues are annoyed, and I just feel this terrible guilt because I can't seem to just dial it back. I want to be a supportive husband and a reliable teacher, but this... this engine inside me just won't shut off, and it's really starting to fray my relationships.\n\nDoctor: Have you always been this way, even as a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Yes. Without a doubt. I mean, it's really important to me that you understand this isn't just... it's not just some reaction to recent stress, you know? Like, it's not something that just started happening with this big family change, with my mother-in-law moving in and all the extra caretaking responsibilities that my wife and I are juggling now. No, no, no. This has been me since day one. \n\nMy mother, she actually used to have this running joke about me when I was just a little guy in elementary school. She'd go to the parent-teacher conferences and come back and tell everyone that I practically taught the class from my seat. Though, honestly, I say \"from my seat,\" but the reality was I was almost never actually sitting in it! I was always up, always wandering around the room, talking to the kids next to me, or—and this sounds exactly like what I do now with my co-teachers, which is tough to think about—but I was always cutting in before the teacher even finished giving directions. \n\nLike, she’d be halfway through explaining a math worksheet or a spelling assignment, and I’d already be blurting out the next step or talking over her because I just... I couldn't hold it in. I was just so eager to get to the doing part. I'd be out of my chair, leaning over someone else's desk, just constantly engaged, constantly in motion. \n\nSo, yeah, this... this constant energy, this way of being, it was a fundamental part of who I was long, long before adulthood. It's literally the story of my life. I remember even into middle school and high school, it was the exact same thing. Always the kid who couldn't just sit quietly and listen. It’s just... it’s always been this way. I’ve always had this motor running, always had to be in the mix. So, no, it's definitely not a new development or some mid-life crisis thing. It's just how I've been wired my entire life.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like your need to be constantly active and moving has significantly interfered with your ability to function effectively in your daily life or relationships?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I mean... like I was just pouring my heart out about a minute ago, it really, really has. I mean, \"significantly\" is probably the exact right word for it, unfortunately. \n\nIt’s just like I was saying about work. That corrective action plan I mentioned? That's not just a casual slap on the wrist. That’s a formal process. It goes in your file, you know? It means I have to sit down every single week with administration and have someone essentially grade my ability to just... be in a room with other professionals. And the worst part of it, the part that honestly just eats at me, is that I feel like I'm completely damaging the trust I’ve built with my colleagues over the years. I've worked with some of these general ed teachers for a decade, and now they look at me like I'm a bull in a china shop. Like I'm a liability instead of a co-teacher. And I'm just trying to help! I see a situation, I want to fix it, but now I’m realizing that my way of helping is actually tearing down those professional relationships. \n\nAnd then I go home, and it's the exact same story. Like I told you, with my mother-in-law living with us, the caregiving routine is incredibly demanding. It's a tight schedule of pills and meals and mobility help. And my wife... she flat out told me that I make those routines harder. She actually said that people have to manage my energy on top of everything else. Manage my energy! Like I'm one of the kids in my classroom, you know? \n\nIt just breaks my heart because I’m trying so hard to be useful. I’m fixing things around the house, I’m moving around, I’m trying to take the load off her shoulders by doing ten things at once, but instead, I’m just exhausting her. I'm exhausting everybody. So, yes, to answer your question, it is absolutely interfering. It’s interfering with my ability to do my job, it's interfering with my marriage... I just feel like I'm eroding all this trust with my family and my coworkers, even though my only intention in the world is to help them.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your constant need to be active and moving is causing you a lot of personal distress?\n\nPatient: Distress? Oh, God, yes. I mean, distress is almost putting it mildly at this point. It's... it's a heavy, heavy weight that I feel like I'm carrying around from the minute I wake up to the minute I finally manage to fall asleep. \n\nYou know, I wake up every morning, and I have these really great intentions. I can't stop it. \n\nAnd then, at the end of the day, when the house finally quiets down... that's when the distress really hits me the hardest. It's like the extra pressure of her moving in just took all my usual quirks and magnified them into this massive problem that I suddenly can't control anymore, no matter how hard I try.\n\nDoctor: Did you exhibit these behaviors of constant activity and restlessness as a child, before the age of 12?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Oh, wow, family photos or videos from back then? You know, that's... well, no, I don't really have anything like that. I mean, we're talking about the late sixties, early seventies here. It wasn't like today where everyone has a high-definition camera in their pocket and they're recording every single moment of their kid's life, you know, every time they sneeze or take a step. Back then, film was expensive! My dad had this old Kodak camera, the kind with the flash cubes that would spin around and blind you for ten minutes after he took a picture, but he really only brought it out for major holidays—Christmas morning, Easter Sunday, maybe a birthday if we were lucky. 

And even then, it was always these very staged, rigid photos. You know the type—"Stand by the tree, tuck your shirt in, look at the camera, smile, don't blink!" There was no capturing of candid, everyday movement. If I was running around being a terror, my parents were too busy trying to wrangle me to stop and take a picture of it. And as for home videos? Forget about it. We didn't have a Super 8 camera or anything fancy like that. I think my uncle might have had one, but he lived three states away, so we only saw him maybe once every five years.
